newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Exports driving German recovery.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Exports driving German recovery.

text.p: Germany's export-led recovery is picking up but investor confidence remains subdued, a crop of reports said on Monday.

The Economics Ministry said in its monthly report that data for April and May pointed to growth in the current quarter. But wrangling over big tax reforms was holding back investment to ratchet growth up further and boost job creation.
"The willingness to invest is clearly being hampered by the continuing lack of clarity over the final drafting of important government reforms," the report said.

The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) threw a government package of 30 billion marks ($16.9 billion) in tax cuts out of the upper house of parliament this month. The tax reform now faces protracted parliamentary mediation.
The report added: "If these measures...remain blocked in the legislative process, that would mean a major burden on planning to invest and reduces chances for an improvement on the jobs market."
Separately, the RWI research institute said that recovery was taking hold, but was being dampened by government efforts to cut borrowing and qualify for Europe's single currency.

The RWI said it expected growth for 1997 to fall slightly short of the government's target of 2.5 percent. Growth in the formerly-communist east, at two percent, will undershoot the west for the first time since unification in 1990.

Despite the growth shortfall, the RWI expects Bonn to come close enough to the budget deficit target of three percent of gross domestic product this year to enable it to join European monetary union (EMU) on schedule in 1999.

"Sticking precisely to the deficit criterion is not required under the Maastricht treaty, and, considering savings efforts so far, German participation in EMU is not in danger," the RWI, one of six leading research groups, said.
Stronger growth should help ease Germany's unemployment crisis late this year, but only in the west where the jobless rate will average 9.3 percent. In the east the rate is seen at 17.4 percent.
The RWI forecast the number of Germans out of work at 4.3 million this year, or 10.8 percent of the workforce, just down from June's seasonally-adjusted post-war record of 4.4 million.

The Economics Ministry said latest data still supported the view that "the drawn-out deterioration is coming to an end...at least in western Germany". The situation was more bleak in the east, where spending on jobs schemes has been cut back.
The ministry added that the brightest spot on Germany's economic landscape was manufacturing, which grew strongly in April and May -- especially in the east -- thanks to exports.

Commerzbank, in a report on the manufacturing sector, said it expected growth to pick up in the second half of the year to post 3.3 percent growth for 1997 as a whole. It forecast 3.8 percent manufacturing growth in 1998.
But accelerating growth will not stop 150,000 industrial workers from losing their jobs this year, although 30,000 new positions will be created in 1998, Commerzbank said.
The Economics Ministry said construction remains weak, with slow orders and empty property pressuring prices and rents.

Price pressures remain subdued, with annual inflation rising slightly to 1.7 percent in June. Rationalisation efforts by companies and modest pay rounds have also helped to cut unit labour costs, boosting German export competitiveness, it said. ($ = 1.777 German Marks)
